Dover.region: Dover and the White Cliffs of Kent
Dover.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of White Cliffs Country
s1loc: Dover anchors one of England's most iconic stretches of coast, where English Heritage's Dover Castle crowns the cliffs above the town with its medieval Great Tower, the Secret Wartime Tunnels and a Roman pharos that is among the oldest surviving lighthouses in the world. Below, the National Trust's White Cliffs of Dover run east toward the South Foreland Lighthouse, a designated National Landscape that draws visitors across the year to this corner of Kent.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the seafront and the Western Heights, with Samphire Hoe country park reclaimed at the foot of the cliffs giving walking, fishing and wildlife trails beside the Channel. The Fan Bay Deep Shelter tunnels, opened to visitors in 2015, and the guided cliff-top walks toward South Foreland add activity-led days out, while Dover Marina and the beach keep operators busy through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deep in Dover, from the Bronze Age Boat at Dover Museum, over 3,500 years old, to the recently restored Maison Dieu, the town's 800-year-old hall that once gave hospitality to pilgrims. The Grand Shaft staircase on the Western Heights and the Roman Painted House add to a layered story, with events and a busy summer calendar bringing day visitors into the town centre.

The visitor trade rests on a settled base of seafront hotels, the Best Western Plus Dover Marina and guest houses near Dover Priory station, with the Port of Dover working ferry and cruise terminals at the Western Docks. High-speed trains link Dover Priory to London St Pancras in about an hour, and neighbouring Folkestone, Deal and Canterbury widen the day-trip catchment across this stretch of the Kent coast.

Morecambe.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Morecambe Bay
s1loc: Morecambe is the classic Lancashire seaside resort on the great sweep of Morecambe Bay, where the bronze Eric Morecambe statue, unveiled by the Queen in 1999, looks out across the sands toward the Lakeland fells. The Art Deco Midland Hotel, reopened in 2008 after a multi-million-pound Urban Splash restoration, and the half-mile Stone Jetty with its public art and bird-themed games anchor a five-mile promenade that defines the seafront.

The leisure and activity layer runs from Happy Mount Park, with its play areas and gardens at the northern end of the prom, to the wide tidal sands and the RSPB Leighton Moss reserve a short way along the bay, home to the largest reed bed in north-west England. Guided bay walks across the famous sands, cycling along the front and the wildlife of the estuary keep activity operators working through the season.

Heritage and culture run along the front and inland to the ancient village of Heysham, where the ruined St Patrick's Chapel and its rock-cut graves sit on the clifftops above Half Moon Bay. The TERN public-art trail of birds threads the promenade, while the long-planned Eden Project Morecambe on Central Drive, beside the Midland Hotel, promises a major new visitor attraction for the resort.

The visitor trade rests on seafront hotels, guest houses and Bed and Breakfast businesses along the promenade, with the Midland anchoring the upper end and coach and tour operators working the bay. Morecambe railway station links the resort toward Lancaster and the West Coast Main Line, and neighbouring Lancaster, Kendal and Preston widen the day-trip catchment between the Lakes, the coast and the city.

Trowbridge.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west Wiltshire
s1loc: Trowbridge is the county town of Wiltshire, shaped by the West of England woollen-cloth trade and set on the River Biss in the west of the county. The free Trowbridge Museum, housed in the Grade II listed Salter's Home Mill within the Shires Shopping Centre, tells that story across two floors with its mill machinery and social history, anchoring the town's visitor draw close to the central Town Park.

The leisure layer centres on the Town Park beside the Civic Centre, with the River Biss winding through the Biss Meadows Country Park to give towpath and meadow walks on the edge of the town centre. Family days out, riverside trails and the green spaces threading the town keep things busy through the warmer months, with the surrounding west Wiltshire countryside on the doorstep for activity-led trips.

Heritage and culture run through the conservation streets around the Parish Church of St James and the elegant Georgian and Victorian frontages of Fore Street and The Parade. The Victorian former Town Hall, now Town Hall Arts, stages drama, comedy and exhibitions, while the modern Civic Centre hosts events and the town's information point, adding to a lively local arts and events calendar.

The visitor trade leans on town-centre hotels and guest houses such as the Moonraker, with County Hall on Bythesea Road bringing council and business visitors into the town. Trowbridge railway station links the line toward Bath, Salisbury and Westbury, and neighbouring Melksham, Chippenham and Frome widen the day-trip catchment across west Wiltshire and the Somerset border country.
Trowbridge.kit_loc: across the town's museums, parks and heritage sites

Barnstaple.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of North Devon
s1loc: Barnstaple is North Devon's oldest borough and its market town, set on the River Taw where the medieval sixteen-arched Long Bridge crosses the water. The covered Pannier Market, built in 1855, is one of Britain's largest indoor markets, trading local produce, crafts and flowers, while the colonnaded Queen Anne's Walk of 1708, with its Merchant's Pillar and statue of Queen Anne, anchors the historic quay at the heart of the town.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the Tarka Trail, the long network of footpaths and traffic-free cycle routes named for Henry Williamson's Tarka the Otter, which threads out from Barnstaple through the unspoilt Taw and Torridge countryside. Family days out, riverside walks and the green spaces around the town give activity operators steady trade, with the North Devon coast and Exmoor close at hand for seasonal trips.

Heritage and culture centre on the Museum of Barnstaple and North Devon, built in 1872, with its Story of North Devon, North Devon at War and Tarka galleries. The early 14th-century St Anne's Chapel, a Gothic chantry chapel near the parish church, and the historic streets and quays add depth, while the Queen's Theatre and the town's markets and events keep the centre busy through the year.

The visitor trade rests on town-centre hotels, guest houses and Bed and Breakfast businesses, with Barnstaple serving as the gateway for visitors heading to the North Devon beaches and Exmoor. Barnstaple railway station sits at the end of the Tarka Line from Exeter, drawing day-trippers and walkers, and neighbouring Bideford, Tiverton and Exeter widen the catchment across North and mid Devon.

Sidcup.region: Sidcup and the London Borough of Bexley
Sidcup.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Bexley borough
s1loc: Sidcup sits in the London Borough of Bexley, where the 140-acre Lamorbey Park spreads around the Grade II listed Lamorbey House and its 1920s landscape, The Glade, with a large lake, added to the national Register of Historic Parks and Gardens in 1988. The Georgian Sidcup Place of 1743 and the Grade II listed Sidcup Manor House anchor the older heart of the suburb on the edge of south-east London.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Foots Cray Meadows, at around 240 acres the largest open space in the borough, a Local Nature Reserve carrying a Green Flag Award where the listed Five Arches bridge crosses the River Cray. Sidcup Place Park, the green corridors of the Cray valley and family trails through the meadows give walkers, anglers and day visitors plenty of space across the season.

Heritage and culture run through the substantial 18th- and 19th-century houses built when the landed gentry favoured the area, from Sidcup Place and Lamorbey to the lost Foots Cray Place. Nearby, the borough's flagship Tudor mansion Hall Place and its formal gardens at Bexley add a major heritage draw, while the Rose Bruford College at Lamorbey keeps a performing-arts tradition alive in the town.

The visitor trade leans on the green spaces and historic houses of the Cray valley, with Sidcup Place now run as a bar and restaurant in its manor setting. Sidcup railway station links the Bexleyheath line into central London, drawing commuters and day visitors, and neighbouring Eltham, Erith and Bromley widen the catchment across south-east London and the Bexley borough.

Hyde.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Tameside
s1loc: Hyde sits in the Metropolitan Borough of Tameside, on the western slopes of Werneth Low, where the 200-acre Werneth Low Country Park climbs to open moorland with panoramic views across Manchester, Cheshire and, on clear days, into North Wales. The Hyde War Memorial crowns the summit, while the Victorian Hyde Town Hall of 1885 on Market Street, with its clock-tower bell known as Owd Joss, anchors the centre above Market Place.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Hyde Leisure Pool, a lagoon-style pool with a gently shelving beach, an eighty-metre water slide, wave machine and water cannons that make it a year-round family draw. Hyde Park, given to the town by the Ashton sisters and opened in 1904, adds municipal green space close to the centre, while the trails and slopes of Werneth Low give walkers and runners activity across the season.

Heritage and culture run through the Victorian streets and the listed Town Hall, with the heritage of the cotton trade still written into the mills and terraces of the town. Markets in Market Place, community events and the wider Tameside calendar keep the centre busy, while the surrounding Peak District fringe and the green slopes above the town give a backdrop for events and days out across the year.

The visitor trade leans on the country park, the leisure pool and the green spaces of the borough, with pubs, eateries and local hospitality serving visitors around the centre. Hyde Central and Hyde North stations link the town toward Manchester, with tram and bus connections across Tameside, and neighbouring Denton, Ashton-under-Lyne and Stalybridge widen the day-trip catchment across eastern Greater Manchester.

Billingham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Teesside
s1loc: Billingham sits on the north bank of the Tees in the Stockton-on-Tees borough, anchored by the Billingham Forum, a pioneering leisure complex opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1967 and celebrated as the first of its kind in the UK. Reopened in 2011 after a fifteen-million-pound refurbishment, the Forum brings together the Grade II listed Forum Theatre, a swimming pool and the famous ice arena under one roof at the centre of the town.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the Forum Ice Arena, home to the Billingham Stars and the Cleveland Comets ice-hockey sides and host to skating lessons and an annual ice pantomime, alongside the Forum pool and dry sports facilities. John Whitehead Park and the green spaces around the town give walking and play areas, with the wider Teesside countryside and the Tees estuary close at hand for activity-led days out.

Heritage and culture run from the Forum Theatre, which stages drama, comedy, musicals and pantomime, to the annual Billingham International Folklore Festival, which fills the town centre each August with dancers and musicians from around the world and marked its sixtieth anniversary in recent years. The old village around St Cuthbert's Church and the green keep an older story alive beside the planned mid-century town centre.

The visitor trade leans on the Forum, the folklore festival and the events that draw crowds into the town, with hotels and guest houses across the wider Teesside catchment serving visitors. Billingham railway station links the line toward Stockton, Middlesbrough and the coast, with Teesside International Airport a short drive away, and neighbouring Stockton-on-Tees, Middlesbrough and Hartlepool widen the day-trip catchment across Teesside.
Billingham.kit_loc: across the town's leisure, theatre and festival sites
